questions.knowledge_point: Calculating a Limit at Positive or Negative Infinity Using L'Hopital's Rule
questions.worked_solution:
In this case, we have an indeterminate form of type $\frac{\infty }{\infty },$ so applying  L'Hopital's rule yields

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to \infty }\frac{2{x}^{3}-6}{{x}^{2}-4} & ={lim}_{x\to \infty }\frac{[2{x}^{3}-6]^{′}}{[{x}^{2}-4]^{′}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to \infty }\frac{6{x}^{2}}{2x} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to \infty }3x \\  & =\infty .\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating a Limit at Positive or Negative Infinity Using L'Hopital's Rule
questions.worked_solution:
Here the limits of the numerator and denominator are ${lim}_{x\to \infty }{x}^{2}=\infty $ and ${lim}_{x\to \infty }\operatorname{ln}⁡2x=\infty ,$ respectively, so we have the case $\frac{\infty }{\infty }.$

Applying L'Hopital's rule, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to \infty }\frac{{x}^{2}}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2x} & ={lim}_{x\to \infty }\frac{[{x}^{2}]^{′}}{{[\operatorname{ln}⁡2x]}^{′}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to \infty }\frac{2x}{(\frac{1}{x})} \\  & =2{lim}_{x\to \infty }{x}^{2} \\  & =\infty .\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating an Indeterminate Limit of the Form Infinity Divided by Infinity Using L'Hopital's Rule
questions.worked_solution:
Here the limits of the numerator and denominator are ${lim}_{x\to (\pi /2)^{-}}ln\,(\operatorname{sec}⁡x)=\infty $ and ${lim}_{x\to (\pi /2)^{-}}ln\,(\operatorname{cot}⁡x)=-\infty ,$ respectively, so we have the case $\frac{\infty }{-\infty }.$

Applying L'Hopital's rule, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to (\pi /2)^{-}}\frac{ln\,(\operatorname{sec}⁡x)}{ln\,(\operatorname{cot}⁡x)} & ={lim}_{x\to (\pi /2)^{-}}\frac{{[ln\,(\operatorname{sec}⁡x)]}^{′}}{{[ln\,(\operatorname{cot}⁡x)]}^{′}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to (\pi /2)^{-}}\frac{(\frac{\operatorname{sec}⁡x\operatorname{tan}⁡x}{\operatorname{sec}⁡x})}{(-\frac{{csc}^{2}⁡x}{\operatorname{cot}⁡x})} \\  & =-{lim}_{x\to (\pi /2)^{-}}\frac{\operatorname{tan}⁡x\cdot \operatorname{cot}⁡x}{{csc}^{2}⁡x} \\  & =-{lim}_{x\to (\pi /2)^{-}}\frac{\operatorname{tan}⁡x\cdot \frac{1}{\operatorname{tan}⁡x}}{\frac{1}{{sin}^{2}⁡x}} \\  & =-{lim}_{x\to (\pi /2)^{-}}{sin}^{2}⁡x \\  & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating a Limit Using L'Hopital's Rule Twice
questions.worked_solution:
If we plug in $x=-4$ we get the indeterminate form $\frac{0}{0},$ so we apply L'Hopital's rule to find the limit:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to -4}\frac{(x+4)^{3}}{3\sqrt[3]{x+5}-x-7} & ={lim}_{x\to -4}\frac{{[(x+4)^{3}]}^{′}}{{[3(x+5)^{1/3}-x-7]}^{′}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to -4}\frac{3(x+4)^{2}}{(x+5)^{-2/3}-1}.\end{aligned}
$$

This time, the resulting limit still gives the indeterminate form $\frac{0}{0}.$ To find the limit, we apply L'Hopital's rule once again. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to -4}\frac{3(x+4)^{2}}{(x+5)^{-2/3}-1} & ={lim}_{x\to -4}\frac{{[3(x+4)^{2}]}^{′}}{{[(x+5)^{-2/3}-1]}^{′}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to -4}\frac{6(x+4)}{-\frac{2}{3}(x+5)^{-5/3}} \\  & =-9{lim}_{x\to -4}(x+4)(x+5)^{5/3} \\  & =-9(-4+4)\,(-4+5)^{5/3} \\  & =-9\cdot 0\cdot 1 \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating a Limit Using L'Hopital's Rule Twice
questions.worked_solution:
If we plug in $x=0$ we get the indeterminate form $\frac{0}{0},$ so  we apply L'Hopital's rule to find the limit:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{{5}^{x}-1-(\operatorname{ln}⁡5)x}{{x}^{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡5} & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{{[{5}^{x}-1-(\operatorname{ln}⁡5)x]}^{′}}{[{x}^{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡5]^{′}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{(\operatorname{ln}⁡5)\cdot {5}^{x}-(\operatorname{ln}⁡5)}{2\operatorname{ln}⁡5\cdot x} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{{5}^{x}-1}{x}\end{aligned}
$$

This time, the resulting limit still gives the indeterminate form $\frac{0}{0}.$ To find the limit, we apply L'Hopital's rule once again. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{{5}^{x}-1-(\operatorname{ln}⁡5)x}{{x}^{2}\text{ }\operatorname{ln}⁡5} & =\frac{1}{2}{lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{{5}^{x}-1}{x} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{{[{5}^{x}-1]}^{′}}{[x]^{′}} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{(\operatorname{ln}⁡5){5}^{x}}{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\,(\operatorname{ln}⁡5){e}^{0} \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡5}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$
